title: Valid Arrangement of Pairs
statement:
You are given `n` pairs `(start, end)`, all distinct, with `start ≠ end` in every pair. An **arrangement** is a reordering of all `n` pairs such that, for every consecutive couple of pairs, the `end` of the first equals the `start` of the second. In other words, you chain the pairs like dominoes, using each pair exactly once and never flipping a pair.

The input is guaranteed to admit at least one valid arrangement. Many inputs admit several, so print the **lexicographically smallest** one: compare two arrangements pair by pair from the first position, and compare two pairs by `start` first and then by `end`.

Print the arrangement, one pair per line.

**Follow-up:** the interviewer asked for a variation of this problem; explain why such an arrangement exists exactly when the graph (vertices are values, pairs are directed edges) has an Eulerian path, and how Hierholzer's algorithm builds it.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `start` and `end` describing one pair.
outputFormat: Print `n` lines. Line `i` contains the two integers of the `i`-th pair of the lexicographically smallest valid arrangement, separated by a space.
constraints: start ≠ end, and no two pairs are identical
At least one valid arrangement exists (this also keeps recursive solutions within stack limits)

examples.explanation: Both `1 2, 2 1, 1 3, 3 1` and `1 3, 3 1, 1 2, 2 1` are valid. The first is lexicographically smaller because its first pair `(1, 2)` is smaller than `(1, 3)`.
Starting with `(1, 2)` would end at value 2, which has no outgoing pair, leaving the other two pairs unused. The only valid arrangement therefore goes through 3 first and finishes with `(1, 2)`.
Value 1 has one more outgoing pair than incoming pairs, so the chain must start there. From 1 take 2 (smaller), come back to 1 via `(2, 1)`, then go 1 → 3 → 4.

hints: Treat each value as a vertex and each pair as a directed edge; a valid arrangement is an Eulerian path that uses every edge once.
The path starts at the vertex whose out-degree exceeds its in-degree by one. If every vertex is balanced, any vertex with edges can start; the smallest one gives the smallest answer.

Run Hierholzer's algorithm: keep each vertex's outgoing neighbours sorted and always follow the smallest unused one, append a vertex to the result when it has no unused edge left, and reverse the result at the end.
